title: “Bentogypsum”, a phosphoric acid purification residue: Characterization and implications for environmental and human health risk in Gabes (SE Tunisia)
institution: R. B. El Zrelli et al., Journal of Hazardous Materials (Elsevier), vol. 508
summary: Peer-reviewed study of a waste called bentogypsum, produced when the Tunisian Chemical Group purifies phosphoric acid in Gabès and stored in open-air stockpiles. It characterises the waste physically, mineralogically and chemically, then runs a screening-level assessment of environmental and human health risk. Received 24 September 2025, accepted 11 March 2026, published online 13 March 2026. Supplementary tables are not part of the PDF used for this record.

findings.headline: Bentogypsum contains 337 mg/kg of cadmium
findings.summary: The study reports an average cadmium concentration of 337 ± 21 mg/kg in bentogypsum (n = 3). Cadmium is the highest of all trace elements measured in the waste. For comparison, the paper lists 48 mg/kg for phosphate rock, 18 mg/kg for phosphogypsum and 49 mg/kg for phosphogypsum foam from the same industrial site.

sample.type: Composite samples of bentogypsum waste (BG1–BG3; each mixed from 5 sub-samples of about 1.2 kg)
sample.location: Fresh truckload of waste bound for the stockpile, Gabès phosphate fertilizer industrial site (SE Tunisia)
sample.method: Acid digestion (U.S. EPA method 3050B), then ICP-MS for trace elements

findings.limitations: Screening-level characterisation of three composite samples taken from one fresh truckload. It describes the waste itself, not contamination measured in air, water, soil or people. The text and Table 7 round the value slightly differently (336 mg/kg in Table 7).

findings.headline: Bentogypsum ranks highest of four phosphate-industry materials for 10 trace elements
findings.summary: Comparing bentogypsum with phosphate rock, phosphogypsum and phosphogypsum foam from the same industrial site, the paper reports bentogypsum as highest for ten elements: As, Cd, Ge, In, Pb, Re, Se, Sn, Th and Tl. On this basis the authors conclude it should be classified as a hazardous waste.
findings.limitations: For indium the Table 4 values (bentogypsum 0.010, phosphogypsum foam 0.037 mg/kg) do not match the ranking stated in the text. Comparison materials come from the authors' earlier studies.

findings.headline: Bentogypsum is strongly acidic: pH 1.15
findings.summary: The average pH of bentogypsum was 1.15 ± 0.11 (n = 3), lower than phosphogypsum (2.20) and phosphogypsum foam (2.36). The authors state that this strong acidity increases how easily pollutants leach out of the waste and move into the environment.

sample.location: Fresh truckload of waste bound for the stockpile, Gabès phosphate fertilizer industrial site (SE Tunisia)
sample.method: pH meter with electrode, soil protocol ISO 10390

findings.limitations: A laboratory measurement of the waste itself. The link between acidity and leaching is the authors' explanation, supported by literature rather than tested in this study.

findings.headline: Fluoride makes up 13.2% of bentogypsum by dry weight
findings.summary: Fluoride averaged 13.22% of dry weight (13.2 ± 0.6% in Table 3), the highest of the four materials compared (phosphate rock 3.42%, phosphogypsum 1.66%, phosphogypsum foam 2.32%). Sodium oxide (Na2O) was also highest in bentogypsum.

findings.limitations: Screening-level characterisation of three composite samples taken from one fresh truckload. It describes the waste itself, not contamination measured in air, water, soil or people.

findings.headline: Bentogypsum is very fine-grained: median grain size 2.88 µm
findings.summary: Median grain size is 2.88 µm and average grain size 2.71 µm; the paper describes essentially all grains as smaller than 20 µm, in the clayey-silt range. The authors link this fine size to wind-driven erosion and atmospheric transport of the waste.

sample.location: Fresh truckload of waste bound for the stockpile, Gabès phosphate fertilizer industrial site (SE Tunisia)

findings.limitations: The text and Table 1 assign the 63% and 37% shares to different size classes (fine silt/clay), so this record uses only the figures that agree. The wind-transport link is the authors' interpretation; dust was not measured.

findings.headline: Bentogypsum is a mix of calcium sulfates and fluoride-bearing minerals
findings.summary: X-ray diffraction identified gypsum (26.42%), malladrite (24.42%), anhydrite (16.70%), heklaite (15.05%), bassanite (8.95%) and haigerachite (8.10%). Malladrite and heklaite are fluoride-bearing silicates. Bentonite clay, used in the purification step, was not detected in the waste.

sample.location: Fresh truckload of waste bound for the stockpile, Gabès phosphate fertilizer industrial site (SE Tunisia)

findings.limitations: Mineral shares are model-based estimates from the diffraction pattern.

findings.headline: Bentogypsum is kept in open-air stockpiles less than 500 m from urban areas
findings.summary: The authors report that the purification residue has been stored in the open air since the early 2000s, described as temporary storage, on a 2.5-hectare site less than 500 m from urban areas. They add that a planned permanent landfill was cancelled after protests against industrial pollution, so waste continues to be added to the temporary site. They also report no sign at the entrance warning of the waste's dangerousness.
findings.limitations: Site description based on the authors' investigations and observations, partly supported by a Gabès Chemical Group (GCT) audit cited in the paper.

findings.headline: About 730,000 tonnes of wet residue stored since 2005
findings.summary: The authors estimate about 730 × 10³ tonnes of wet bentogypsum stored at the site since 2005, with current production of about 100 tonnes per day (about 36,500 tonnes per year).
findings.limitations: The production rate is the authors' estimate from their own investigations, not an official published figure. The paper's underlying table (Table S.7) is in the supplementary material.

findings.headline: Four pollution indices place bentogypsum in their highest classes
findings.summary: Using six metals (As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Pb, Zn) the paper reports: contamination degree 3899 (very high), pollution load index 14.94 (polluted), geoaccumulation index 46.25 (extremely contaminated) and potential ecological risk index 116,264 (very high). The authors state these exceed the top-class thresholds by about 122, 15, 9 and 194 times respectively.
findings.limitations: Screening indices computed from the waste's composition. Background values come from three soil samples taken at a non-impacted site (Matmata, about 40 km south of Gabès). The authors state the indices do not predict actual ecological damage.

findings.headline: Cadmium accounts for 94.58% of the toxic units
findings.summary: Of the toxic-unit total for the six metals considered, cadmium contributes 94.58%, followed by arsenic (3.44%), chromium (1.37%), zinc (0.30%), lead (0.16%) and copper (0.15%).
findings.limitations: Covers only six metals. Fluorine, rare earth elements and radionuclides were not included in these indices.

findings.headline: Non-cancer hazard index for children: 10.99 (above 1)
findings.summary: For a modelled child, the combined non-cancer hazard index (HI) for six metals is 10.99 ± 0.61. Values above 1 indicate a potential non-cancer health concern in this method. The authors describe children as about 9 times more at risk than adults.
findings.limitations: Screening-level result calculated from the waste's composition with standard exposure assumptions, for modelled people aged 6 (child) and 24 (adult). It is not a measurement of exposure or illness in actual residents.

findings.headline: Non-cancer hazard index for adults: 1.24 (above 1)
findings.summary: For a modelled adult, the combined non-cancer hazard index is 1.24 ± 0.07, slightly above the value of 1 used as the concern level.
findings.limitations: Screening-level result calculated from the waste's composition with standard exposure assumptions, for modelled people aged 6 (child) and 24 (adult). It is not a measurement of exposure or illness in actual residents.

findings.headline: Total cancer risk for children: 2.98 × 10⁻² (limit used: 10⁻⁴)
findings.summary: Table 6 gives a total carcinogenic risk (TCR) of 2.98 × 10⁻² ± 1.81 × 10⁻³ for a modelled child, based on arsenic, cadmium, chromium and lead. The authors compare it with an upper limit of 10⁻⁴ and conclude the waste poses a serious carcinogenic risk.
findings.limitations: Screening-level result calculated from the waste's composition with standard exposure assumptions, for modelled people aged 6 (child) and 24 (adult). It is not a measurement of exposure or illness in actual residents. The running text gives 9.98 × 10⁻² and a factor of 289 for children, which does not match Table 6; the table value, which equals the sum of its components, is used here.

findings.headline: Total cancer risk for adults: 3.20 × 10⁻³ (32 times the 10⁻⁴ limit)
findings.summary: Table 6 gives a total carcinogenic risk of 3.20 × 10⁻³ ± 1.95 × 10⁻⁴ for a modelled adult, which the authors state is 32 times the 10⁻⁴ upper limit they use.
findings.limitations: Screening-level result calculated from the waste's composition with standard exposure assumptions, for modelled people aged 6 (child) and 24 (adult). It is not a measurement of exposure or illness in actual residents.

findings.headline: Swallowing is the dominant exposure route in the risk calculation
findings.summary: In the modelled scenarios, ingestion accounts for 98% of cancer risk for both children and adults, with skin contact about 1.4% (children) and 1.7% (adults) and inhalation under 0.05%. For non-cancer risk, ingestion accounts for 70% (children) and 66% (adults), skin contact 29% and 32%, and inhalation 0.20% and 0.51%.
findings.limitations: Screening-level result calculated from the waste's composition with standard exposure assumptions, for modelled people aged 6 (child) and 24 (adult). It is not a measurement of exposure or illness in actual residents. Route shares depend on the exposure assumptions in the paper's supplementary tables, which are not part of the PDF used for this record.

findings.headline: Cadmium drives most of the calculated health risk
findings.summary: Across all exposure routes, cadmium accounts for 68% of the non-cancer risk for children and 70% for adults, and for 92% of the cancer risk for both children and adults.
findings.limitations: Screening-level result calculated from the waste's composition with standard exposure assumptions, for modelled people aged 6 (child) and 24 (adult). It is not a measurement of exposure or illness in actual residents.

findings.headline: The landfill liner is torn and sinking in places, with no leachate treatment
findings.summary: The authors describe a 1.5 mm HDPE geomembrane over about 20 cm of compacted clay, installed in 2005, with a drainage ditch but no leachate treatment system. They report greenish drainage water standing around the piles, tearing of the geomembrane and localized subsidence (Fig. 7), and say heavy rain makes polluted water overflow.
findings.limitations: Based on the authors' field observations and photographs.

findings.headline: Authors estimate the waste's weight far exceeds what the liner can bear
findings.summary: The authors state that the vertical stress from the waste is about 30 t/m², about 14 times the typical tensile strength and about 7 times the puncture threshold they cite for a 1.5 mm HDPE geomembrane, and propose this as an explanation for the damage seen.
findings.limitations: An estimate by the authors using inputs in supplementary Table S.7, which is not part of the PDF used for this record. They also suspect the liner is punctured below the surface, which is a hypothesis, not an observation.

findings.headline: Stockpiles about 12 m high with little dust protection; summer winds from the east and northeast
findings.summary: The authors report stockpiles about 12 m high, protected only by a wall about 3.5 m high and a sparse vegetation screen, and say there is no other protection against dust. They state prevailing summer winds come mainly from the E and NE, and that contaminated dust is likely carried toward inhabited and cultivated zones near the site.
findings.limitations: Dust and wind transport were not measured in this study; the transport direction is the authors' inference. The paper says quantifying off-site exposure at different distances would need dedicated monitoring.

findings.headline: Authors say leachate may reach groundwater used for drinking and irrigation
findings.summary: The authors state that the liner does not effectively stop drainage water from infiltrating the sandy bedrock and reaching groundwater, which they say neighbouring inhabitants of Chatt Sidi Abd Essalam use for irrigated fields and for drinking water. They describe groundwater contamination as the second main pathway, after wind-blown dust.
findings.limitations: The paper's main text reports no groundwater or leachate measurements. This is a stated pathway and risk, not a confirmed contamination result.

findings.headline: Authors report illnesses among neighbours, but no epidemiological study exists
findings.summary: From field observations (asking inhabitants and factory workers), the authors report cases of serious non-cancer illnesses and cancers, mainly lung, bone, prostate and kidney, among people living near the dumpsite. They say the illnesses may be related to exposure to bentogypsum-derived contaminants, but that other untreated industrial wastes act in combination with it, that the exact exposure pathways have not been fully studied, and that no epidemiological study has yet been carried out despite repeated local requests.
findings.limitations: These are informal observations reported by the authors, not a systematic health study, and they do not show that bentogypsum caused the illnesses.

findings.headline: The risk assessment is a screening, not a prediction of illness
findings.summary: The authors state that the indices are a tier-1 screening of the waste's intrinsic hazard under plausible exposure scenarios. They do not aim to predict actual disease or ecological damage. The paper also notes the lack of site-specific toxicological and epidemiological data.
findings.limitations: This is the paper's own account of its scope. Its data are stated to be available on request.

findings.headline: Authors conclude bentogypsum is hazardous waste and call for urgent action
findings.summary: The authors conclude that bentogypsum should be classified as hazardous industrial waste, not an inert by-product. They recommend containment and isolation of existing stockpiles, leachate and dust control, treatment or stabilization strategies, a ban on on-site storage near urban and agricultural areas, and similar assessments at other phosphoric acid plants.
findings.limitations: The authors' conclusions and recommendations. They are not a regulatory decision.
